title: India Bars ISRO Scientists From Quitting as Brain Drain Threatens Gaganyaan and Key Space Missions
excerpt: More than 100 scientists have left ISRO in recent months, many joining private space startups, prompting the government to strip centre directors of authority to approve resignations.
body:
• The Department of Space issued a July 14 memorandum barring routine acceptance of resignations from scientists working on Gaganyaan and other flagship missions
  • Between 100 and 120 scientists and engineers have left ISRO in recent months, with roughly 80 departing from the U R Rao Satellite Centre alone
  • Many departing scientists are joining India's booming private space sector, which now includes over 400 registered startups with nearly $500 million in total investment
  • The exodus includes senior figures such as the LVM-3 project director and a Chandrayaan-3 team member, raising concerns about institutional knowledge loss

Government Reverses 2020 Policy, Centralises Exit Decisions

The Department of Space has issued an internal memorandum, dated July 14, that fundamentally changes how India's premier space agency handles staff departures. Under the new directive, resignation and voluntary retirement requests from Group 'A' scientific and technical personnel working on Gaganyaan and other nationally important missions will no longer be processed at the centre level. Instead, each request must be forwarded to the Department of Space itself for final approval.

The order reverses an administrative change introduced in 2020 that had delegated approval authority to directors of individual ISRO centres, including the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), and the Satish Dhawan Space Centre. Centre directors must now defer such requests until ongoing projects are completed and submit each case with their recommendations to the department.

"The U R Rao Satellite Centre in Bangalore, which designs and builds India's satellites, has been hit hardest with approximately 80 departures."

"The U R Rao Satellite Centre in Bangalore, which designs and builds India's satellites, has been hit hardest with approximately 80 departures."

"The growing number of resignation and voluntary retirement requests from Group 'A' scientific and technical personnel has begun affecting the timely implementation of projects of national importance."

— Department of Space internal memorandum, July 14, 2026

The Scale of the Exodus

According to reports by The Times of India and Outlook Business, between 100 and 120 scientists and engineers linked to ISRO's most critical programmes have left the agency in recent months. The U R Rao Satellite Centre in Bangalore, which designs and builds India's satellites, has been hit hardest with approximately 80 departures. The Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre in Thiruvananthapuram, responsible for launch vehicle development, has lost at least 20 more.

The departures are not limited to junior staff. Named exits include the LVM-3 project director Victor Joseph from VSSC — a role directly tied to the Gaganyaan human spaceflight programme — the SpaDeX project director from URSC, and a young scientist who had been part of the Chandrayaan-3 lunar landing team. The Department of Space's vacancy rate has reached a 25-year high, with nearly three in ten posts lying vacant.

Private Space Boom Fuels the Drain

The exodus is closely linked to the rapid growth of India's private space sector. Since the government opened the space industry to private companies in 2020 and implemented the Indian Space Policy in 2023, more than 400 space startups have been registered in the country. These firms have collectively attracted nearly $500 million in investment, including approximately $150 million in 2025 alone.

Companies such as Skyroot Aerospace, which successfully launched India's first private orbital rocket this week, Pixxel, Dhruva Space, Agnikul Cosmos, and Bellatrix Aerospace have emerged as well-funded employers offering significantly higher compensation than government pay scales. Former ISRO Chairman S. Somanath himself joined Chennai-based Agnikul Cosmos as a board observer after completing his tenure in January 2025.

What This Means for India's Space Ambitions

The timing is particularly concerning for Gaganyaan, India's first crewed spaceflight mission, which represents the country's most complex and high-stakes space endeavour. The programme requires sustained expertise across propulsion, life support systems, and crew safety — areas where institutional knowledge is difficult to replace.

ISRO has also faced technical challenges recently. The PSLV-C62 mission in January deviated from its planned trajectory following a third-stage malfunction, and the Drishti satellite lost contact after a solar storm.

The government's response — effectively blocking resignations rather than addressing pay disparities or working conditions — has drawn mixed reactions. While it protects mission continuity in the short term, critics argue it could further demoralise remaining staff and make ISRO a less attractive employer for new talent entering a job market where the private space sector offers both better pay and faster career progression.
